blocks.h: This chapter provides the regulatory and bibliographic infrastructure for the entire work. It contains five distinct reference resources:

• Section 39.1–39.6: A topic-indexed reference guide to the principal regulatory instruments cited throughout this book, organised by Act with subject-matter cross-references to the relevant chapters.
• Section 39.7: Selected Nigerian judicial decisions on insurance contracts — the case law foundation for insurance contract interpretation in Nigeria.

• Section 39.8: An annotated bibliography organising all sources cited or recommended throughout the 36 content chapters into five categories: Books and Monographs; Academic Journal Articles; Regulatory and Industry Publications; International Sources; and Online Resources and Data.

rows: Signed 6 August 2025. Came into force on assent except where specific provisions set a later commencement date for specific requirements (e.g., transitional capital compliance timelines).

Repeals and replaces the Insurance Act, Cap I17, Laws of the Federation of Nigeria 2004 (originally the Insurance Act 2003). Provisions of the repealed Act inconsistent with NIIRA 2025 are extinguished; regulations and guidelines made under the repealed Act that are not inconsistent remain in force until replaced.
National Insurance Commission (NAICOM) — established under the NAICOM Act 1997, which continues in force, with NIIRA 2025 expanding NAICOM’s powers and mandate.
Federal Republic of Nigeria Official Gazette; naicom.gov.ng; National Assembly of Nigeria (nassnigeria.gov.ng).

blocks.h: The following index maps the principal subject-matter areas of NIIRA 2025 to the parts and sections of the Act most relevant to each topic, with cross-references to the chapters of this book where each topic is discussed in depth. Section numbers are indicative based on the Act’s published structure; practitioners should verify against the official Gazette version.

rows: Licensing of insurers and capital requirements

Part II and Part IV: Licensing provisions; capital thresholds in s.15: life ₦10 billion, non-life ₦15 billion, reinsurance ₦35 billion (or risk-based capital if higher). The Act provides no composite insurer licence (s.6); Takaful and Insurtech thresholds come from NAICOM regulation.
Part III: Solvency and capital adequacy. RBC replaces the fixed-percentage minimum solvency margin. Insurers must maintain RBC at or above the NAICOM-prescribed ratio. ORSA required annually.
Part IV: All new products and material modifications must be submitted to NAICOM for approval before marketing. Grounds for NAICOM to withhold approval; timelines for response.
Part IV: The statutory codification of the principle that coverage does not commence until the first premium is received by the insurer.
Part V: Mandatory group life at a minimum of 3× annual emoluments for employers with qualifying workforce (cross-references PRA 2014). Mandatory credit life for qualifying loans.

Consumer protection provisions: duty of disclosure and the s.65 limits on repudiation, s.17 policy-document delivery and s.209 misleading statements are in the Act; the TCF mandate, complaint rights, cooling-off period and plain-language requirement come from NAICOM regulation and guidelines.

Part VI: Settlement of valid claims within 60 days of notification (s.210), with compound interest for each month of delay and administrative sanctions. [Verify: a 5-business-day acknowledgement period is not confirmed in the Act.]

Part VI and Part VIII: Licensing of agents (s.37: certificate of proficiency, 10 years’ underwriting experience) and brokers; s.38 agents may not collect premium; s.62 maximum commission rates (group life 9%, single-premium annuity 3%).

Part VIII: Two licensing tracks — Partnering Insurtech (₦10 million capital) and Standalone Insurtech (₦1–1.5 billion capital, depending on product class). Regulatory sandbox provisions. Cybersecurity requirements for Insurtech licensees.
Part IX: Requirements for conventional insurers to establish Takaful windows; separate fund maintenance; Shari’ah Supervisory Board requirement; standalone Takaful licensing.

Part X: Obligation to offer a defined proportion of reinsurance to domestic reinsurers before international placement. Life and non-life domestic cession percentages. NAICOM approval for international facultative placements above threshold.

Part XI: Board composition (minimum 5 directors, NED majority, minimum 2 independent directors, Chair/CEO separation). Fit and proper requirements. Board committees. Statutory Actuary independence. Three lines of defence.
Part XII: NAICOM admissible asset framework. Restrictions on connected-party investments. ALM requirements for long-duration life and annuity business. Investment Policy Statement approval.
Part XIII: Insurance sector AML/CFT obligations; KYC requirements; suspicious activity reporting to the Financial Intelligence Unit; MLPPA 2022 compliance.
Part XIV: Insurers as data controllers under NDPA 2023. Obligations consistent with the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 and GAID 2025. Data breach notification. Policyholder data rights.

Part XV: NAICOM powers to inspect, investigate, impose administrative fines, suspend or revoke licences, appoint receivers, and disqualify directors. Market conduct inspection framework. Whistleblower protection.
Part XVI: Internal dispute resolution requirements. NAICOM Consumer Protection Bureau complaint handling. Insurance Ombudsman framework. Escalation to courts.
Part XVII: Transitional timelines for recapitalisation compliance, agent qualification under Cert. COP, and other provisions requiring lead time for implementation.
NAICOM Guidelines for Technology-Driven Insurance Operations in Nigeria (Insurtech Guidelines), 2025
1 August 2025 (preceding the formal commencement of NIIRA 2025 by days, co-ordinated for simultaneous practical effect).
Subsidiary regulation issued by NAICOM under powers conferred by NIIRA 2025. Legally binding on all licensed insurers and Insurtech licensees.

Applies to: (1) Licensed insurers operating digital insurance platforms or partnering with technology companies; (2) Partnering Insurtech licensees (₦10m capital); (3) Standalone Insurtech licensees (₦1–1.5bn capital depending on product class); (4) Companies seeking regulatory sandbox admission.

Minimum capital: ₦10 million (NAICOM Insurtech guidelines; not in the Act). Partnering Insurtechs must partner with a fully licensed insurer that retains the insurance risk. The Insurtech performs distribution, technology, or processing functions only. Cannot assume underwriting risk on own account.

Minimum capital: ₦1 billion to ₦1.5 billion (NAICOM Insurtech guidelines; not in the Act). May hold the insurance licence and assume risk on own account. Subject to all NIIRA 2025 capital, solvency, governance, and product approval requirements that apply to conventional licensed insurers.
Applications for sandbox admission: purpose, scope, timeline (maximum 24 months), consumer protection safeguards required, reporting obligations during sandbox period, exit pathway to full licensing.

All Insurtech and digital insurance operations must implement: encryption standards for policyholder data; multi-factor authentication; penetration testing (minimum annual); incident response plan; data breach notification to NAICOM and affected policyholders within 72 hours.

Insurtechs may not: make binding underwriting decisions without licensed insurer involvement; pay claims directly from operating accounts (claims funds must be segregated); conduct unsolicited direct marketing without valid consent under NDPA 2023; apply algorithmic pricing based on protected characteristics.

AI and ML models used in underwriting, pricing, or claims must be: documented (model development, training data, validation); validated by a qualified actuary or risk professional before deployment; monitored for drift and bias on a defined schedule; approved for use in regulated functions by NAICOM on request.

The licensed insurer (not the embedding partner) is responsible for product approval, claims obligations, and policyholder communication. Embedding agreements must be disclosed to NAICOM. Policyholders must receive clear disclosure of the insurer’s identity.
USSD-based and mobile-distributed insurance products must comply with product approval requirements. Premium collection through mobile money platforms requires documented reconciliation controls.

blocks.text: 39.3 Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 (NDPA 2023) and GAID 2025

rows: Signed 12 June 2023 by President Bola Tinubu.
Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) — established by the Act as the independent data protection authority.

Licensed insurers are expressly classified as ‘Data Controllers and Data Processors of Major Importance’ due to the volume and sensitivity of personal health, financial, and biometric data they process.
General Application and Implementation Directive 2025 (GAID) — the primary implementation directive under the NDPA 2023.
ndpc.gov.ng; Federal Republic of Nigeria Official Gazette.

Insurers must identify a lawful basis for each category of personal data processed: contract necessity (policy administration); legal obligation (AML/KYC); legitimate interest (fraud prevention); consent (marketing communications). Consent must be specific, informed, freely given, and revocable.

Health data collected for underwriting and claims purposes is a ‘special category’ requiring heightened protection. Must be processed under explicit consent or another specific permitted ground. Strict access controls required.

Policyholders have rights to: access their personal data; correct inaccurate data; erasure (‘right to be forgotten’ — subject to legal retention requirements); portability; restriction of processing; objection to direct marketing. Insurers must have documented processes for responding to data subject requests within 30 days.

Insurers must notify the NDPC within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach likely to result in risk to data subjects. Notification to affected data subjects required where the breach creates high risk to their rights and freedoms.

Insurers must conduct DPIAs before implementing new high-risk processing activities — specifically including: AI/ML underwriting models; biometric data processing; large-scale health data processing; data sharing with third parties outside Nigeria.

Personal data of Nigerian data subjects must be stored on servers located in Nigeria (primary storage) unless the Data Commissioner grants an exemption or the transfer is subject to appropriate safeguards.

Insurers must not retain personal data longer than necessary for the purpose for which it was collected. Minimum retention periods for insurance data are specified in GAID 2025 (claims records: minimum 10 years; policy records: 7 years after policy expiry).
Compliance as Data Controller of Major Importance (NDPA 2023)
Annual NDPC filing; mandatory appointment of a Data Protection Officer (DPO); mandatory Data Protection Compliance Programme (DPCP) reviewed and submitted to the NDPC; mandatory audit every 2 years.

The PRA 2014 creates the insurance industry’s two most significant mandatory product markets: (1) mandatory group life insurance for employers; and (2) the Retirement Life Annuity (RLA) as one of two CPS decumulation options. The PRA 2014 is therefore the single most important piece of external legislation for life insurance practitioners after NIIRA 2025 itself.

Every employer with 3 or more employees must maintain a minimum group life insurance policy providing a death benefit of not less than 3× the total annual emoluments of each employee. Failure to maintain the group life policy is an offence. The policy must be maintained with a NAICOM-licensed insurer.

The mandatory defined-contribution pension system for employees in organisations with 3 or more staff. Employer contribution: minimum 10% of monthly emoluments. Employee contribution: minimum 8%. Contributions must be remitted to the employee’s Retirement Savings Account (RSA) managed by a licensed PFA within 7 working days of salary payment.

Each CPS participant has an individual RSA managed by a PFA of their choice. The RSA is portable across employers. PFAs must provide RSA statements at least quarterly. PFAs invest RSA funds in NAICOM/PenCom-approved asset classes.

On retirement (or reaching 50 years with reduced capacity), an RSA holder may: (1) withdraw up to 25% of the RSA balance as a lump sum; (2) use the balance to purchase a Retirement Life Annuity from a NAICOM-licensed life insurer; or (3) elect Programmed Withdrawal administered by the PFA.

An RLA must provide: a guaranteed lifetime income; an option for joint life coverage for a surviving spouse; inflation protection option. The RLA insurer is required to meet NAICOM’s solvency margin requirements. PenCom and NAICOM jointly regulate the RLA market.

On death of an RSA holder before retirement: the accumulated RSA balance is payable to the designated beneficiaries. If the employer’s group life insurance has been maintained, the group life death benefit is paid separately and is in addition to the RSA balance.

Failure by an employer to: deduct and remit employee contributions; maintain mandatory group life; or enrol employees in the CPS — exposes the employer to criminal prosecution, fines, and civil liability for any resulting loss to the employee.

CPS members may make additional voluntary contributions to their RSA above the mandatory minimum. VCs are tax-deductible under PITA (Personal Income Tax Act). Insurers offering PPP products may position them as complementary to the VC mechanism.

blocks.text: 39.5 Other Principal Legislative and Regulatory Instruments

blocks.h: The NAICOM Act establishes the National Insurance Commission as Nigeria’s apex insurance regulator and sets out its constitution, powers, and functions. Key provisions: NAICOM’s corporate status and governance; the Commissioner for Insurance and the NAICOM Board; NAICOM’s powers of inspection, investigation, and enforcement; the NAICOM Establishment Fund; appeals from NAICOM decisions. The NAICOM Act is read together with NIIRA 2025, which expands NAICOM’s regulatory mandate without replacing the NAICOM Act.

The Chartered Insurance Institute of Nigeria Act establishes CIIN as the professional body for insurance in Nigeria. Key provisions: CIIN’s corporate status; the CIIN Council and its composition; the CIIN’s examination, membership, and disciplinary functions; the power to award qualifications and confer membership grades; the CIIN’s role in setting professional standards for the Nigerian insurance market. NIIRA 2025 cross-references CIIN qualifications as the minimum professional standard for regulated insurance roles.

blocks.text: 39.5.3 National Health Insurance Authority Act 2022 (NHIA Act)

rows: Signed 19 May 2022. Repeals and replaces the National Health Insurance Scheme (NHIS) Act 1999.

Establishes the legal framework for universal health coverage in Nigeria; licences and regulates Health Maintenance Organisations (HMOs); sets standards for benefit packages, provider contracting, and claims management in the health insurance market.

Sections 9–15: HMO licensing requirements and conditions. Sections 26–30: Minimum benefit standards and claims processing obligations. Section 41: The NHIA’s enforcement powers including licence suspension and revocation. Section 48: The mandatory health insurance initiative for States, applying the universal health coverage mandate.
2015 (as amended by the Cybercrimes Act (Amendment) Act 2024).

Criminalises unauthorised access to computer systems (relevant to cyber intrusions targeting insurer policy and claims databases); electronic fraud (relevant to digital insurance fraud, false online claims, identity theft); cyberstalking and harassment (relevant to digital insurance distribution); phishing and social engineering (relevant to insurer customer data protection).

Section 6: Unlawful access to computer systems — criminalises any access without authorisation to an insurer’s PAS or customer database. Section 14: Identity theft and impersonation using computer systems — relevant to synthetic identity fraud in digital insurance. Section 22: Electronic fraud — covers false online insurance claims. Section 38: The Cybercrimes Advisory Council’s role in national cybersecurity coordination.

The Cybercrimes Act provides the criminal law overlay for cybersecurity incidents that are separately regulated by NIIRA 2025 (operational risk requirements), the NAICOM Insurtech Guidelines (cybersecurity standards), and the NDPA 2023 (breach notification obligations).

blocks.h: CAMA 2020 is the primary Nigerian corporate law, applying to all registered companies including life insurers. Key provisions for life insurers: the obligation to maintain company registers (directors, members, charges); directors’ duties (fiduciary, care, skill); the annual general meeting and shareholder rights; requirements for company secretarial compliance; the insolvency and winding-up regime applicable when NAICOM has revoked a licence; the statutory merger and acquisition framework applicable to insurance company consolidations.

The MLPPA 2022 is the primary AML/CFT legislation applicable to financial institutions including insurers. Key provisions: the duty to conduct customer due diligence (CDD) and enhanced due diligence (EDD) for high-risk customers; the obligation to monitor transactions and report suspicious activities to the Nigerian Financial Intelligence Unit (NFIU); record-keeping obligations (minimum 5 years); the penalties for failure to comply (fines, deregistration, criminal prosecution of directors). NIIRA 2025 cross-references the MLPPA 2022 for all AML/CFT obligations applicable to licensed insurers.

blocks.text: 39.5.7 Personal Income Tax Act (PITA) — Selected Insurance Provisions

rows: Life insurance premiums paid by individuals for their own life insurance policies are deductible for PITA purposes up to statutory limits. Employer-paid group life premiums are deductible business expenses.
Voluntary contributions to an RSA under the PRA 2014 are fully tax-deductible under PITA, creating a significant tax incentive for the PPP and VC market.

Death benefits under a life assurance policy are generally not taxable income in the hands of the beneficiary. Maturity benefits and surrender values from endowment and savings-linked policies may be subject to tax on the gains element — practitioners should advise clients to seek tax advice.
Lump sum critical illness benefits are generally regarded as capital receipts and not subject to income tax.

blocks.text: 39.7 Selected Nigerian Judicial Decisions on Insurance Contracts

blocks.h: Nigerian courts have developed a body of case law interpreting insurance contracts that is essential background for insurance practitioners. The following selected decisions address the principal legal issues arising in insurance practice: the duty of disclosure, insurable interest, claims settlement, exclusion clauses, and the interpretation of policy terms. Cases are cited in the standard Nigerian citation format: [Year] NWLR Part Page or (Year) FWLR Part Page.

rows: Adesanya v. Royal Exchange Assurance Nigeria Ltd
The duty of utmost good faith requires the proposer to disclose all material facts, whether asked or not. Non-disclosure of a material fact entitles the insurer to avoid the policy.

Establishes the breadth of the disclosure obligation in Nigeria: it is not limited to answering the proposal form’s specific questions but extends to any information a prudent insurer would consider material.
African Continental Bank Ltd v. Nigerian General Insurance Co. Ltd
A misrepresentation in a proposal form, even if innocent, entitles the insurer to avoid the policy if it relates to a material fact.
Confirms that the materiality test is objective (would a prudent insurer consider it material?) not subjective (did the proposer consider it important?).
The insurer bears the burden of proving that the undisclosed fact was material and that the non-disclosure induced the making of the contract.
Important for claims disputes: the insurer cannot invoke non-disclosure as a defence without demonstrating materiality and inducement.
Nigerian Agricultural and Co-operative Bank Ltd v. NICON Insurance Corporation
A creditor has an insurable interest in the life of a debtor to the extent of the outstanding debt.
Establishes the basis for credit life insurance in Nigerian law: the lender’s insurable interest is limited to the outstanding loan balance, not the full life of the borrower.
Chief Omonuwa v. Insurance Company of Nigeria Ltd
A spouse has an insurable interest in the life of the other spouse. The interest is unlimited in both directions.
Foundation case for spousal life insurance in Nigeria. Confirms that husband and wife each have unlimited insurable interest in the other’s life.
Leadway Assurance Company Ltd v. Zeco (Nig.) Ltd
Insurance policies must be read as a whole. Ambiguous terms are construed against the insurer (contra proferentem rule).
Affirms the contra proferentem doctrine in Nigerian insurance law: where a policy term is ambiguous, the interpretation least favourable to the insurer (who drafted the document) prevails.
IGI Plc v. Kalu Industries Ltd

An insurer cannot reject a valid claim on technical grounds unrelated to the substance of the loss. A purported rejection without valid legal basis amounts to wrongful repudiation entitling the insured to damages.

Critical for claims management: the case establishes that insurers must have substantive legal grounds for repudiation; technical defences unrelated to the merits of the claim do not justify non-payment.
NEM Insurance Company (Nig.) Ltd v. Aderibigbe
Notice of claim must be given within the period specified in the policy. Failure to give timely notice may bar recovery where the insurer can demonstrate prejudice from the delay.
Establishes the standard for late claim notification: mere delay is not sufficient to bar a claim; the insurer must show that the delay prejudiced its ability to investigate or manage the loss.
A beneficiary designation in a life insurance policy overrides inconsistent instructions in the policyholder’s will.
Confirms the primacy of the policy nomination over testamentary disposition for life insurance benefits — critical for financial planning advice and estate planning.
An insurer that delays settlement of a valid claim beyond the contractual period is liable for the principal sum plus interest at the court’s discretion from the date the claim became due.
Post-NIIRA 2025, the 60-day mandatory settlement period supplements this case: an insurer that fails to settle within 60 days faces both NAICOM enforcement and potential court-ordered interest.

blocks.h: The following bibliography organises the sources cited and recommended throughout this book into five categories. Annotations identify the primary value of each source for Nigerian insurance practitioners and students, and the chapters of this work for which each source is most relevant.

blocks.text: A. Books and Monographs — Insurance, Risk, and Finance

blocks.h: Actuarial Education Service (ActEd). Subject SP2: Life Insurance. Institute and Faculty of Actuaries. acsedservices.com.

The primary study text for the IFoA life insurance actuarial examination. Comprehensive actuarial treatment of life insurance product design, reserving, ALM, and ERM. Essential for actuarial staff and for readers seeking deep technical actuarial understanding. [Chapters: Chapters 10, 13, 23, 31]
Bernhardt, D. (ed.). Competitive Intelligence: How to Acquire and Use Corporate Intelligence and Counterintelligence. Financial Times Prentice Hall, 2003.

The standard reference for competitive intelligence methodology. Covers legal and ethical intelligence gathering, field intelligence systems, and intelligence report design. Applied to the CI function design in Chapter 36. [Chapters: Chapter 36]
Black, K. Jr. and Skipper, H. Life and Health Insurance. 13th edn. Prentice Hall, 2000.

A comprehensive global reference for life and health insurance product structures, actuarial principles, and regulatory frameworks. Though published pre-NIIRA 2025, its foundational treatment of life insurance concepts remains definitive. [Chapters: Chapters 10–15, 25, 30–33]
Borch, K.H. The Economics of Insurance. North-Holland, 1990.

The foundational economic theory of insurance: the theory of risk, the economics of the insurance firm, and the welfare economics of insurance markets. Essential background for advanced practitioners. [Chapters: Chapter 1]
Bromiley, P. and Rau, D. Strategic Management. SAGE, 2016.
Corporate strategy reference covering competitive analysis, strategic planning, and strategic implementation. Applied to the strategy and research function in Chapter 27. [Chapters: Chapter 27]
Edmondson, A.C. The Fearless Organization: Creating Psychological Safety in the Workplace for Learning, Innovation, and Growth. Wiley, 2018.

Research-based text on organisational culture, psychological safety, and the conditions required for disclosure culture and effective risk escalation. Applied to the discussion of non-disclosure culture in Chapter 35. [Chapters: Chapter 35]
Galbraith, J.R. Designing Organizations: Strategy, Structure, and Process at the Business Unit and Enterprise Levels. 3rd edn. Jossey-Bass, 2014.

The definitive text on organisational design: functional, matrix, and hybrid structures; spans of control; coordination mechanisms. Applied to Chapter 34’s treatment of insurance company organisational structures. [Chapters: Chapter 34]
Gitman, L.J. and Joehnk, M.D. Personal Financial Planning. 14th edn. Cengage Learning, 2017.

Standard personal financial planning reference. The life cycle approach to insurance, savings, and retirement planning informs Chapter 25’s treatment of personal financial planning within the insurance context. [Chapters: Chapter 25]
Harrington, S.E. and Niehaus, G.R. Risk Management and Insurance. 2nd edn. McGraw-Hill, 2004.

Comprehensive insurance economics and risk management text. Addresses the principles of insurance, moral hazard, adverse selection, and the design of insurance contracts. Foundational for Chapters 11–15. [Chapters: Chapters 11–15]
Kaplan, R.S. and Norton, D.P. The Balanced Scorecard: Translating Strategy into Action. Harvard Business School Press, 1996.
The source text for the Balanced Scorecard framework applied to insurance strategy measurement in Chapter 27. [Chapters: Chapter 27]
Keller, S. and Meaney, M. Leading Organizations: Ten Timeless Truths. PublicAffairs, 2017.

McKinsey’s synthesis of organisational performance research. Addresses talent, culture, capability, and leadership — all applied to Part Seven’s treatment of the life insurance enterprise. [Chapters: Chapters 34, 35]
Kenny, D.A. and others (eds). Reinsurance Practice and the Law. Informa Law from Routledge, 2019.

The primary practitioner reference for reinsurance law and practice. Covers treaty structures, facultative placements, claims under reinsurance, and cross-border reinsurance regulation. [Chapters: Chapter 14]
LOMA. FLMI Programme Study Materials. loma.org.

The Fellowship, Life Management Institute (FLMI) programme materials cover all aspects of life insurance management — products, underwriting, claims, operations, marketing, governance — from the insurer management perspective. [Chapters: All chapters]
Mintzberg, H. Structure in Fives: Designing Effective Organizations. Prentice Hall, 1992.
Classic organisational theory covering the five structural configurations and their determinants. Informs the treatment of functional vs. matrix structures in Chapter 34. [Chapters: Chapter 34]
Mishkin, F.S. The Economics of Money, Banking and Financial Markets. 12th edn. Pearson, 2018.

Standard financial economics reference. The treatment of financial institutions, risk management, and asymmetric information provides the economic foundation for insurance market analysis. [Chapters: Chapters 1, 23]
Porter, M.E. Competitive Advantage: Creating and Sustaining Superior Performance. Free Press, 1985.
The foundational competitive strategy text. Porter’s Five Forces, value chain analysis, and competitive positioning framework inform the strategic analysis in Chapter 27. [Chapters: Chapter 27]

blocks.h: Ahuja, R. and Jutting, J. ‘Design of Incentives in Community Based Health Insurance Schemes.’ CESifo Working Paper. ifo Institute for Economic Research, 2003.

Nigeria’s primary macroeconomic and demographic data source. Essential context for insurance market sizing, segmentation, and forecasting. [Chapters: All research-related chapters]
NIA (Nigerian Insurers Association). Annual Industry Statistics Report. nianetwork.com.
The primary public source for market-level premium income, loss ratio, and investment data across NIA member companies. [Chapters: Chapters 21, 36]
PenCom (National Pension Commission). Annual Report; RSA Statistics; PFA Market Share Data. pencom.gov.ng.
The authoritative source for CPS market data including RSA balances, PFA performance, and RLA market statistics. [Chapters: Chapters 31, 33, 36]
NHIA (National Health Insurance Authority). Annual Reports; HMO Register. nhia.gov.ng.
Regulatory and market data for the Nigerian health insurance sector. [Chapters: Chapters 32, 36]

blocks.text: D. International Research and Reference Sources

blocks.h: AXCO Insurance Information. Nigeria Country Report (updated annually). axcoinfo.com.
Country-specific regulatory, market, and product data for Nigeria. A subscription-based starting point for insurance market intelligence and regulatory navigation. [Chapters: Chapter 36]
Geneva Association. Research Papers and Geneva Papers on Risk and Insurance. genevaassociation.org.

The world’s leading insurance industry think tank. Publishes research on insurance economics, climate risk, longevity, digital transformation, and regulatory developments. Open access research papers and the Geneva Papers journal. [Chapters: All chapters]
IAIS (International Association of Insurance Supervisors). Insurance Core Principles (ICPs); Global Insurance Market Report (GIMAR). iaisweb.org.

The global standard-setting body for insurance regulation. The ICPs provide the framework within which NIIRA 2025 is designed. The GIMAR provides global insurance market statistics for comparative benchmarking. [Chapters: Chapters 15, 21, 24, 36]
IMF. Global Financial Stability Report; Nigeria Article IV Consultation Reports. imf.org.
The IMF’s biannual financial stability assessment and annual Nigeria country review. Essential macroeconomic context for insurance market planning. [Chapters: Chapter 36]
Munich Re. Topics Magazine; NatCatSERVICE; Life and Health Reinsurance Research. munichre.com.
Comprehensive insurance research across catastrophe risk, life/health reinsurance, and African market developments. [Chapters: Chapters 14, 15, 36]
OECD. OECD Insurance Statistics; OECD Principles of Corporate Governance. oecd.org.

Global insurance market statistics and governance standards. The OECD Principles of Corporate Governance are the global baseline referenced in Chapter 34’s governance discussion. [Chapters: Chapters 24, 34, 36]
Swiss Re Institute. Sigma Publication Series; African Insurance Reports. swissre.com/research.

The most widely cited commercial insurance research publications globally. Sigma provides annual global market statistics; thematic reports cover digital insurance, climate risk, microinsurance, and emerging market development. [Chapters: All chapters, particularly 28, 36]
World Bank. Global Financial Development Database; Financial Sector Assessment Programme (FSAP) Nigeria Reports. worldbank.org.
World Bank financial sector development data and Nigeria FSAP assessments of the insurance regulatory framework. [Chapters: Chapters 22, 36]

blocks.title: A Note on Currency and Verification

blocks.h: This regulatory reference index reflects the Nigerian insurance regulatory landscape as at the date of this work’s publication. The Nigerian insurance regulatory framework is evolving rapidly — NIIRA 2025 is itself the most comprehensive reform of the Insurance Act in more than two decades, and it is followed by an active programme of subsidiary regulation from NAICOM.
Practitioners should apply the following verification practices:
• For regulatory provisions: always verify against the current Gazette version or the NAICOM circular register before relying on a provision in practice.
• For case law: verify citations against the original law reports or the Supreme Court and Court of Appeal databases before citing in formal advice or legal proceedings.

• For market data: access the most recent available publication of each primary data source (NIA, NAICOM, EFInA, NBS, PenCom) rather than relying on the data figures cited in this work, which reflect the period of research.
